articles.title: Net dollar purchases more than halve in October as hedging curbs support rupee
articles.summary: Mumbai: Net dollar purchases in the forwards market more than halved through October from the previous month to about $17 billion as targeted regulatory curbs on hedging took effect, building stability in the value of the rupee that surged from the end of the month to anchor a stunning revival of overseas interest in India-listed growth assets.The Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), brought in to dissuade unnecessary currency hedging amid a haemorrhage that even record hauls from forex-inflow programmes couldn't seemingly staunch, immediately reduced dollar purchases in the forward market in October to $49 billion from $76 billion in September, CCIL data showed.135906856Dollar sales, meanwhile, reduced to $32 billion from $41 billion, marking a broader reduction in dollar demand that stood in sharp relief against a steady climb in the dollar index over the past four weeks. The dollar climbed 1.5% against a basket of six heavily traded currencies through this period, while the removal of state oil retailers' demand from the spot market and absence of unnecessary hedging provided the spot rupee the cushion it needed to draw in overseas funds.Read more: Indian equities ride global AI trade unwind: Is D-Street back on foreign investors' radar? BNP Paribas answers"Overall hedging has gone down after FERR and things have got more stringent. So, hedging happens only for what is required," said Sajal Gupta, head of forex and commodities at Nuvama. "Importers are hedging on a short-term basis while exporters still feel that the weakness in the rupee may reappear and are holding back on hedging."Read more: Ahead of Market: 10 things that will decide stock market action on TuesdayHedging demand over the last few years has contributed to increased dollar demand, with importers hedging more and exporters hedging less.The rupee has recovered since mid-October, after touching near 97 levels last month. It closed at 93.92 on Monday, and has gained more than 3% from its record low levels.'Weakness Bias'The gap between forward dollar purchases and sales widened to $233 billion in FY26 from $97 billion in FY24, indicating a substantial increase in net dollar demand arising from hedging activity. Importers increasingly hedged amid expectations of sustained rupee deprecation, while exporters reduced their dollar sales, thus increasing dollar demand.FERR increased importer hedging costs by requiring banks to park 20% of the rupee value of eligible forward contracts with the RBI in non-interest-bearing cash reserves. This raises banks' funding and opportunity costs, which are passed on to importers through higher hedging charges, making forward dollar purchases more expensive."However, the effectiveness of FERR will depend on how long importer hedging remains curtailed. If the expectation of continued rupee depreciation persists, then importer hedging could pick up," said Gaura Sengupta, chief economist, IDFC First Bank.

articles.title: Indian equities ride global AI trade unwind: Is D-Street back on foreign investors' radar? BNP Paribas answers
articles.summary: Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have returned to Indian equities with purchases worth nearly $8 billion over 15 trading sessions, as global investors reassess their exposure to AI-linked stocks, offering a fresh boost to Dalal Street after nearly two years of sustained foreign selling. Between October 21 and November 10, foreign investors bought approximately $8 billion worth of Indian equities, reversing around 16% of the nearly $50 billion they had sold over the preceding two years, according to a report by BNP Paribas.The renewed foreign buying has coincided with a strong recovery in domestic equities, with the benchmark Nifty50 gaining around 10% over the past one month."The return of foreign capital comes against the backdrop of significant selling in other Asian markets. FIIs sold $9 billion worth of equities in South Korea and $26 billion in Taiwan, while major regional indices came under pressure. Over the 30-day period cited in the report, the Nasdaq declined around 7%, South Korea's KOSPI fell 16% and Japan's Nikkei dropped 10%.ALSO READ: Coal India's 3rd big windfall in a year? How Mahanadi Coalfields IPO could unlock Rs 8,964 croreBNP Paribas said India was capturing a portion of the global portfolio rotation away from the AI theme. The investment bank attributed the shift to concerns over whether returns on capital would justify the substantial expenditure on AI infrastructure and the possibility of a slowdown in AI spending."The recent decline in AI-linked equities appears driven by market concerns regarding the scale of returns on capital relative to significant capital expenditures and expectations of a slowdown in AI spending," the brokerage said.The shift in global flows has coincided with an improvement in India's domestic macroeconomic environment. Crude oil prices have declined, US 10-year Treasury yields have eased from 5.3% to around 5.1%, and multiple rating agencies have upgraded their GDP growth forecasts for India.The rupee's appreciation against the US dollar has also supported foreign investor returns. BNP Paribas noted that the USD/INR exchange rate moved from 95.8 to 94.3, further enhancing dollar-denominated returns for FIIs.The improvement in investor sentiment has also been reflected in market performance. The Nifty gained around 10.5% over the past month, significantly outperforming the midcap index, which rose 3.7%, and the smallcap index, which gained just 0.5%.IT, telecom lead initial foreign buyingThe initial return of foreign investors was concentrated in the information technology and telecommunications sectors.ALSO READ: Saw the rally coming? How India's mutual funds raised stakes in 11 Nifty stocks before rebound to gain bigAccording to BNP Paribas, NSDL data showed that FII buying in the second half of October was heavily concentrated in these two sectors. Foreign investor holdings in Indian IT stocks increased to $45 billion in October from $37 billion in September, while telecom holdings rose to $39 billion from $35 billion.However, the report noted that market performance in November indicated that the rally had started broadening beyond these sectors into the wider largecap universe.FII holdings in Indian equities stood at $685 billion in October, marginally lower than $689 billion in September, indicating that the recent return of buying had yet to translate into a meaningful month-on-month increase in overall holdings.Largecaps emerge as beneficiariesThe return of foreign investors has coincided with a shift in domestic investor preferences towards largecap stocks, providing an additional source of support to the segment.Flows into pure largecap mutual funds increased around 20% month-on-month to Rs 10 billion in October, while inflows into large and midcap funds surged 99% to Rs 85 billion. In contrast, growth in inflows into midcap and smallcap funds decelerated by 38% and 29%, respectively.BNP Paribas said, "We continue to prefer large caps," arguing that the segment was benefiting from the twin tailwinds of FII buying and retail investors shifting allocations away from small- and midcap-oriented schemes.The investment bank added that the convergence of foreign and domestic buying was providing a significant advantage to largecap valuations."We observe a twin tailwind for Indian large-cap stocks driven by shifting investor flows," the brokerage said, adding that the convergence of FII and retail buying was providing a significant advantage to largecap valuations.Valuations are also relatively more attractive in the largecap segment. The report puts largecap valuations at 18.4 times price-to-earnings, compared with 23.1 times for midcaps and 21.8 times for smallcaps.Largecap earnings growth of around 20% year-on-year in the second quarter of FY27 has also helped narrow the earnings growth gap with smaller companies.Domestic flows remain supportive, but liquidity is tighteningWhile foreign investors have returned, domestic institutional investors (DIIs) have continued to play an important role in supporting the market.DIIs bought $6.5 billion worth of equities in October, even as FIIs sold $2.2 billion during the month. However, domestic mutual fund flows moderated, with overall equity scheme inflows declining 14% month-on-month to Rs 330 billion in October. Systematic investment plan (SIP) inflows remained relatively stable, declining 1% to Rs 321 billion.At the same time, mutual fund cash holdings declined to $18.4 billion, or 3.8% of assets under management, the lowest level since July 2024.BNP Paribas described the shift in domestic investor allocations as a "flight to quality", adding that the rotation from SMID stocks towards largecaps, alongside increased inflows into liquid funds, suggested that investors were becoming more cautious.The brokerage noted that 95% of bond fund inflows were concentrated in liquid and money market funds, indicating a growing preference for cash management.The report also flagged elevated equity supply, with IPOs and qualified institutional placements remaining high for the third consecutive month.Despite the moderation in mutual fund flows, retail participation remained visible, with 3.4 million new demat accounts opened during the month, the highest monthly addition since January 2026.However, the ratio of discontinued or completed SIPs to new registrations increased to 1.17, with new SIP registrations falling to 5.1 million and discontinued SIPs rising to 5.9 million.BNP Paribas cautioned that a sustained reading above one in the SIP stoppage ratio could be negative for future SIP flows.The return of foreign investors, therefore, comes at a time when domestic flows remain substantial but signs of tightening liquidity are emerging within the mutual fund industry.Disclosure: This article has been written by Kumar Gaurav, who is not a Sebi-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.title: India's sugar output more than doubles to 2.35 mn tonnes by Nov 15: ISMA
articles.summary:
India's sugar production more than doubled to 23.59 lakh tonne in the ongoing 2026-27 season through November 15, as mills in top producer Maharashtra started crushing early, the Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) said on Monday.
Output stood at 11.49 lakh tonne in the same period a year earlier, the industry body said. The sugar season runs from October to September, with crushing typically starting in October-November.
The sweetener's production in Maharashtra, the country's biggest producer, jumped more than threefold to 18.51 lakh tonne from 5.25 lakh tonne a year earlier. Mills in the western state began crushing from October 8, earlier than in other states, and 154 mills were operating as of November 15, against 132 a year ago.
Output in Uttar Pradesh, the second-biggest producer, fell to 2.10 lakh tonne from 4.25 lakh tonne, with 80 mills operational compared with 88 a year earlier.
In Karnataka, the third-largest producer, output was little changed .

articles.summary:
A terrorist was killed while another was trapped in an encounter with security forces in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district where three CRPF personnel were injured in an attack last week, police said on Monday.
"Encounter with terrorists started in Kulgam," the Kashmir Zone Police said in a post on X.
The police said the whole area has been cordoned off with the help of the army and other security forces.
Officials identified the trapped terrorists as Lateef Bhatt and Umar. While the body of one terrorist was visible, efforts were on to neutralise the second terrorist.
The two terrorists were involved in the attack on a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) post in the same district last week.
All the nearby units of the army and elite Special Operation Group of the Jammu and Kashmir Police were involved in the encounter.
